III · Adoption · two variables

From cheap equipment to installed power

Incumbents = those who own and run the existing electricity system. Financing = who pays the up-front cost, and at what interest rate.

III · Adoption · incumbency

Lock-in

The deep-rooted interests of traditional energy industry in countries’ domestic political, economic, and social systems have caused the situation of carbon lock-up, which prompts traditional energy beneficiaries to resist energy transition … Yang, Xia & Qian 2023: 690
… green industrial policy can break carbon lock-in by broadening the coalition for change. Allan, Lewis & Oatley 2021: 6 (Depth reading)

Carbon lock-in = when existing fossil-fuel investments, jobs and rules make switching costly for those who benefit from them.

III · Adoption · five terms

Glossary

Dispatch
The order in which the grid operator buys power from plants each hour. Plants first in line sell the most power.
Curtailment
Telling a solar or wind farm to switch off because the grid can’t carry its power. The energy is simply lost.
Net metering
The meter runs backward: power a rooftop owner sends to the grid is credited at the same price they pay for grid power. Net billing pays them a lower, wholesale price instead.
Capacity payments
Fixed fees a utility pays a power plant for being available, whether or not its power is used.
Cost of capital
The interest rate or return investors demand to put up money. For solar and wind, almost all costs are paid up front, so this rate largely sets the price of the power.

III · Adoption · incumbency · the tools

How incumbents shape adoption

  • Dispatch rules: whose power plants the grid buys from first MEXICO
  • Auctions and permits: whether private builders can get contracts at all MEXICO
  • Grid connection: whether a new plant or rooftop is allowed to plug in PAKISTAN · GREECE
  • Buy-back rates (“net metering” / “net billing”): what a rooftop owner is paid for power sent to the grid PAKISTAN · KENYA
  • Import taxes on panels PAKISTAN
  • Guaranteed-payment contracts: utility pays private plants whether or not their power is used PAKISTAN

Case sources on the Thursday slides.

Discussion · 25 minutes

Questions

  1. Every case uses largely Chinese panels at historically low prices. Using incumbency and financing, explain why Mexico’s solar share stayed near 7% while Pakistan’s tripled.
  2. Pakistan and Kenya both limited what rooftop owners are paid for power sent to the grid. Make the case for that policy, then the case against it.
  3. Uzbekistan’s buildout was financed and built mostly by foreign developers and banks. Compare with Mexico, where a strong state utility held private builders back. What does each case say about Nem Singh’s call to rethink state capacity?
